summary: EARTHVERSE is an interactive web app that makes real NASA data understandable, and honest about its limits. Earth Mode lets anyone compare six real NASA-ISRO NISAR L-band radar observations of the Karachi coast and Indus Delta (July to October 2026) with a swipe slider. It automatically warns when two images are not directly comparable, for example when they were processed differently. Cosmos Mode shows real NASA SPHEREx infrared sky images and compares the same patch of sky at two wavelength ranges, warning when images look at different places. Discovery Lab is an AI science guide that adapts to a learner-chosen level (from ages 5 to adult), answers questions about the exact images selected, and runs quizzes whose answers are checked on the server. Every page separates what was observed, how it is shown, a cautious interpretation, and what still needs verification, so radar and infrared data become approachable without overclaiming. Public understanding of Earth observation grows when people can explore real data and learn its limits.
details:
What it does. EARTHVERSE has three parts. Earth Mode compares six real NISAR L2 GCOV radar preview images (one orbit track, 24 days apart) with a swipe or side-by-side view. It reads each scene’s metadata and warns the visitor, for example when one scene came from a different processing run. Cosmos Mode shows three real SPHEREx Quick Release 2 spectral images from one exposure, and checks from the pointings whether two images show the same patch of sky. Discovery Lab is an AI science guide. The learner picks a level (Little Explorers to Curious Adults), and the guide answers about the exact images chosen. A quiz keeps its answer keys on the server, with hints and retries.

Why it matters. Satellite data is powerful but easy to over-read. Every analysis page separates Observed data, Visualization, Possible interpretation and Needs verification, and the app never claims a difference proves a cause. SPHEREx is never linked to Earth-surface changes.

How it’s built. Next.js, React, TypeScript and Tailwind CSS, hosted on Vercel. Python (astropy, numpy, Pillow) converts SPHEREx FITS files. NASA’s ASF DAAC search service supplies the NISAR previews and metadata. The AI guide calls the IFM K2 model from the server, with automatic fallback to prepared answers, and the app supports several AI providers.

Responsible design. There are no accounts, cookies or camera use. Questions containing personal details are blocked before reaching the AI, the learner’s level is a choice and never guessed, and every AI answer is labelled as AI-generated and not a NASA finding.

Limits. The radar images are previews, not full-resolution data, and no change map is computed. The cause of one bright band in an infrared image is unexplained, and the page says so. AI answers can be wrong.
